what: Build Check Part 2 (wording check), statements version 0.2, 8 October 2026. Only the statements that changed since the version before were checked again.

statements_checked.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements_checked.text: In the UK, the main pruning is done in late winter or early spring, in February or March. Two rose growers say January or February, and one garden company says on a frost-free day between November and March. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements_checked.text: In the south of the UK, do the main pruning around mid-February. In northern and colder areas, wait until March; one garden company says mid to late March. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements_checked.text: In the UK, do the main pruning in February or March. For the Midlands and the south of England, one rose nursery says November or December instead. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the Midlands and the south of England only

statements_checked.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements_checked.text: In northern and colder areas of the UK, wait until March for the main pruning. For the north of England and Scotland, one rose nursery says between January and late February instead. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the north of England or in Scotland only

statements_checked.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements_checked.text: Prune on a frost-free day, before new growth begins and the buds start to open. One source says to prune when growth is just resuming.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements_checked.text: Two rose growers say a rose can be trimmed in autumn, between September and November, so that winter wind does not rock or damage it. One of them says this is for tall roses, and that autumn is too early to cut a rose back hard. Months are only a guide.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: Which months do I prune my rose?
statements_checked.text: One rose grower says not to cut a rose back hard in autumn, because frost can then damage the cut tips.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements_checked.text: Give the first feed in spring, in March or April, before the rose flowers. One rose grower says towards the end of February or in early March. Months are only a guide.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements_checked.text: Feed the rose again in mid-summer, after its first round of flowers. One rose grower says in July. Months are only a guide.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: When do I start and stop feeding?
statements_checked.text: One rose grower says to give the last feed before the end of August, so that the rose can slow down for winter and frost does not damage new growth. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements_checked.text: Deadhead (remove the faded flowers) while the rose is in flower, through summer and into autumn. One rose grower says to keep deadheading in October. Months are only a guide.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements_checked.text: If your rose is grown for its hips (the rose's fruit), stop deadheading in time for the hips to form. One source says to stop in mid-summer, and one rose grower says after the second round of flowers.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: When do I stop deadheading?
statements_checked.text: Apart from roses grown for hips, I couldn't find a month to stop deadheading in the UK. A local rose society is the place to ask.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: In the UK, plant a bare-root rose (one sold without soil on its roots) while it is dormant (not actively growing), between October and early March. Months are only a guide.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: Don't plant a bare-root rose while the ground is frozen. One rose grower says to keep it in a bucket of water or compost until the ground has thawed.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: A rose in a pot can be planted at any time of year, as long as the ground is not frozen, waterlogged or very dry. One garden company says the ideal months are September to November and March to May. Months are only a guide.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: One rose grower says not to plant a potted rose in extreme heat.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: Which months do I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: Move an established rose while it is dormant, between November and February. One source says shrubs that drop their leaves in winter can be moved at any time from late October to mid-March. Months are only a guide.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements_checked.text: Clear away fallen rose leaves in autumn, so that disease has nowhere to linger. One source says to destroy them, or bury them under a layer of mulch (material spread over the soil).
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements_checked.text: One rose grower says to pick up fallen leaves and cut off diseased leaves in October and November, and to tidy the beds in February, ready for spring. Months are only a guide.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements_checked.text: One source says to pick off any leaves still on the rose over the winter months, if practical, and dispose of them, to help against black spot.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements_checked.text: One rose grower says to check the base of your rose for exposed roots before the winter weather takes hold, and to build up a layer of mulch around any that show, to protect them from the cold.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements_checked.text: I couldn't find UK advice from a gardening body or rose society on spraying roses in winter. A local rose society is the place to ask.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: When do I clear up and spray in winter?
statements_checked.text: I couldn't find UK advice on mounding soil over the base of a rose for winter. A local rose society is the place to ask.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: How do I allow for frost and my own garden?
statements_checked.text: On average, the last frost of spring comes earlier in southern and coastal parts of the UK, often before the end of April, the national weather service says. Further north and on higher ground it often comes well into May, and in a few places in June. Late frosts still happen, so months are only a guide.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

statements_checked.question: How do I allow for frost and my own garden?
statements_checked.text: Frosts go on later in spring on an exposed, rural or high site than near the coast. In a valley, cold air drains downhill and pools overnight, so frost is especially likely there.
statements_checked.shown_to: Gardeners in the United Kingdom only

results.note: The suggested wording is used as given. Supported as before (RHS-MB, LTG-PR); it now says the south of the UK and the main pruning.

Now leads with the better-supported months (AF-1, High), gives the nursery second and as one source, and is marked as a disagreement, so rule 2 and section 3A are met. Still shown only in the six regions. The trace exists and AF-5 is now used as one side of a disagreement. It repeats the opening of item 1 for the same gardener, which it must do to stand alone.

The words pass: March leads (AF-3, Moderate; RHS-MB, LTG-PR), the nursery is second and said as one source, and it is marked as a disagreement. One slip in the trace: it cites C-9, and C-9 as written is only about the south ('STYLE prunes in November and December in the Midlands and south'). The northern clash, the nursery's January to late February against 'wait until March', is not written into any conflict. Add it to C-9 (or to C-1, which version 0.1 cited here). No change to the words.

'Cut a rose back hard' is a fair plain rendering of 'hard prune'. One small thing: the statement now says 'autumn is too early', while the corrected AF-9 says the grower 'says October is too early' (PB-OCT). Autumn as a whole is confirmed, but on PB-WF, which belongs to AF-16, and AF-16 is not in this trace. Either add AF-16 to the trace and keep the words, or say October.
results.suggested_wording: Two rose growers say a rose can be trimmed in autumn, between September and November, so that winter wind does not rock or damage it. One of them says this is for tall roses, and that October is too early to cut a rose back hard. Months are only a guide.

results.note: Still true to PB-WF ('not recommended to hard prune them during the autumn though as the tips can then become damaged by frost'). 'Cut a rose back hard' is plain and says no more. C-14 exists and is rightly traced here.
The suggested wording is used as given (PB-FEB: 'Towards the end of February or in early March').
'First round of flowers' is a fair plain rendering of 'first flush of flowers' (RHS-GG, HARK-EG, PB-FEED) and adds nothing.
'Early' is gone; 'in time for the hips to form' is RHS-GG's 'to give the hips time to form'. 'Second round of flowers' is a fair rendering of DA-DH's 'second flush'.

The new opening stops this gap from seeming to contradict item 2, and the gap is still true (AF-35). Two small points. Read on its own, 'hips' is not explained here. And 'Apart from roses grown for hips, I couldn't find a month' suggests a month was found for those roses; what was found is a season and a round of flowers (RHS-GG mid-summer, DA-DH after the second flush), not a month.
results.suggested_wording: For a rose that is not grown for its hips (the rose's fruit), I couldn't find a month to stop deadheading in the UK. A local rose society is the place to ask.

results.note: The meaning of bare-root is now given, in the words already published in PKR-CGD-000016, and I checked that the published statement carries the same trace (ARC-BUSHROSE-PLANTMOVE-01 AF-1). The rest is unchanged and supported.
The suggested wording is used as given. True to RHS-MOVE ('Deciduous plants: Move at any time during the dormant season from late October to mid-March'), and said as one source.
The suggested wording is used as given (PB-NOV: 'cut off any diseased leaves').
The black spot purpose is now said, as on RHS-BS. 'Black spot' is the spelling Pip's published answers use.

Cut back to what was confirmed: exposed, rural or higher sites (RHS-FROST), high ground and the coast (MO-FROST), valleys (MO-FROST). The sheltered and town part is gone, and AF-31 is reworded to match.

package_notes: Result for the 14 changed statements: 11 pass, 3 pass with a note, none fail. The two earlier fails are cured. I also checked that the 12 statements not listed are unchanged from version 0.1, that every trace exists, that labels match, and that the project's own validator reports OK.

C-9 as written covers only the south. The nursery's months for the north of England and Scotland against 'wait until March' are not in any conflict's words, though item 4 now traces C-9. Widen C-9 or add the northern months to C-1.
C-14 cites PB-CAL and PB-OCT. The sentence that was confirmed for 'not in autumn, because the tips can be damaged by frost' is on PB-WF; add PB-WF to C-14.
p8/uk_notes.md is still out of date on the nursery: it says AF-5 is used as local months, labelled Very Low, with the south counties said in the UK-wide statement. None of that is so in version 0.2.

findings_comments.comment: The wording is now right. The limitation still says 'The sheltered, urban and coastal part ... is not confirmed word for word', while the finding now rests the coast on MO-FROST's confirmed sentence. Take 'coastal' out of that sentence of the limitation so the two agree.

The statement no longer says 'early', but the finding still says 'deadheading stops early so that the hips can form'. Neither RHS-GG nor DA-DH says 'early'. Say 'deadheading stops so that the hips can form'.
